title: Carved hazel jam spoon
subtitle: Green-wood spoon-carving from a straight hazel billet
excerpt: A small jam spoon carved from a fresh hazel billet. Narrow bowl, short handle, light in the hand. A good first green-wood spoon because hazel billets split cleanly and carve without resistance.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the spoon-blank progression from riven billet; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the general axe-to-knife method.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Carves easily under hand tools and shapes well before it dries.
A short length of split timber, ready to be shaped into a blank and then a finished item.
The rough-shaped piece of wood from which the finished spoon is carved.
A short straight-bladed knife with a stout handle; the Swedish school-craft standard for whittling and spoon-carving.
A curved-bladed knife for hollowing the bowl of a spoon or kuksa.
A leather strap charged with abrasive compound, used to maintain a sharp edge between honings.

content.text: A hazel jam spoon is a small, narrow-bowled spoon for spreading jam, honey, or soft cheese, the kind that sits in a jar or on a board. Hazel grows straight, splits cleanly along the grain, and carves without the resistance you get from oak or beech. As a first green-wood spoon this one earns its place: the billet is easy to source, the blank shapes quickly, and the finished spoon is useful.
This project uses
green wood
throughout. Green hazel carves so easily that many makers use only a sloyd knife and a hook knife with no axe at all.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
What you need
Wood
One straight hazel
billet

, roughly 20 cm long and 4, 5 cm across. Split straight from a coppice rod or a branch up to thumb-thickness above the intended length. Hazel is food-safe when finished with a drying oil. The alternative is birch: same carving properties, slightly paler in colour. Cherry carves a little harder but takes a finer finished edge.

Source fresh hazel from a local coppice, community orchard prunings, or a tree surgeon's off-cuts. The billet should be freshly cut or stored in water and used within a few days. If the cut end has already darkened and dried at the rim, trim 2 cm off before splitting.
Tools
Sloyd knife
for shaping the handle and outside of the bowl.
Hook knife, small, for hollowing the bowl.
Leather strop
with stropping compound, use it every fifteen minutes.
Carving axe (optional): useful for roughing the blank quickly, but a sloyd knife alone is sufficient for a hazel billet of this size.
240-grit sandpaper (optional): for smoothing the bowl interior if the hook-knife finish is uneven.
Raw linseed oil for finishing.
Workspace

A low stool or a garden chair with your knees at a comfortable working height. Good light from the side so the surface relief is visible. No children or pets within arm-and-blade reach. If you are using the axe, a low splitting block at shin height is the right surface; for the knife work alone, your lap with a folded leather apron is enough.
The work
Step 1: Split the billet and mark the blank
Split the billet in half through the pith with a knife and mallet or a splitting wedge. One half becomes the
blank
. Draw the spoon profile on the flat face in pencil: the bowl is roughly 4 cm long and 2 cm wide, set about 2 cm from the tip end; the handle runs the remaining 14 cm.
Step 2: Rough out the plan shape

Using the sloyd knife, make a series of push cuts down the sides of the blank to remove the waste wood outside the pencilled outline. Hold the blank in a four-finger grip on the work, knife hand above, blade travelling away from the thumb toward the tip of the blank into open air.
Push cuts
are the right choice here: the blade is travelling away from the body along the long axis of the blank. Work both sides until the plan shape is clean.
Step 3: Shape the back of the bowl
Turn the blank over so the flat face (future inside of the bowl) is down. Use push cuts and
thumb-pivot cuts

to carve the back of the bowl into a smooth dome. The bowl back on a jam spoon is shallow, the lowest point is no more than 5 mm below the shoulder of the handle. Check this often by holding the spoon at eye level along its length: you want a gentle curve, not a deep hollow. On hazel, the grain runs straight; cuts in either direction along the length of the blank are safe. Cuts across the grain at the waist (where the handle meets the bowl) need attention: go with the grain from the bowl toward the handle on that shoulder, not against it, or the blank will chip at the join.
Step 4: Hollow the bowl
Turn the blank flat-face up. Use the
hook knife

, small, to hollow the bowl. Begin at the centre and work in small arcs, drawing the hook toward you with the work held steady in the other hand. The blade should peel thin shavings, not dig in. A sharp hook knife takes curls of wood about the thickness of a fingernail; if you are getting thick chunks, the edge needs stropping. Keep the hollow shallow for a jam spoon, a depth of about 3 mm at the centre is enough. The walls should be even; uneven walls mean the spoon will dry unevenly and may crack.
Step 5: Refine the handle

Use push cuts and thumb-pivot cuts to taper the handle from the shoulder down to a comfortable grip width at the end, roughly 8 mm across. A slight faceting on the sides of the handle is both traditional and practical: it prevents the spoon rolling off a table. Decide how much bark to keep before you start the handle: a ring of bark at the end of the handle is a common hazel-spoon signature, and the bark is stable once the spoon is oiled.
Step 6: Check and strop

Hold the spoon at eye level and sight down its length. The bowl should be centred on the handle axis. Run a thumbnail along the inside of the bowl: the surface should feel even with no ridges. Strop both the sloyd knife and the hook knife before the finishing cuts. A finishing push cut along the outside of the bowl, blade at a very shallow angle to the surface, taking the thinnest possible shaving, brings the surface to a near-finished state.
Finishing
Let the spoon dry for two to three days before finishing. If the bowl shows any small check cracks after drying, lightly sand the interior with 240-grit paper folded around a dowel.

Apply raw linseed oil liberally. Let it soak in for one hour, then wipe off the surplus with a clean cloth. Repeat after twenty-four hours, then leave to cure for two weeks before food contact. Raw linseed oil is food-safe once fully cured; do not rush the cure time. Spread the oiled rag flat to dry, not crumpled, linseed-soaked rags can smoulder if bunched up.
Variations
Honey spoon: make the bowl rounder and slightly deeper, with a wider, flatter tip, to allow honey to drip slowly from the bowl.
Left-handed version: the bowl hollow is centred regardless of handedness. Only adjust the handle grip if a centred position feels awkward.
Birch or cherry: birch gives a paler finish; cherry darkens over time with use to a warm red-brown. Both food-safe under raw linseed.
Care
Wash by hand with warm water. Dry with a cloth immediately, do not leave to soak. Re-oil every few months or when the wood starts to look dry. Never put in a dishwasher.

attrs.symptom: The blank splits along the grain when roughing out
attrs.cause: Cutting across the grain at the waist where handle meets bowl
attrs.fix: Always cut with the grain at the shoulder, from the wider bowl toward the narrower handle, not against. Recheck grain direction by looking at the side of the blank before each cut.

attrs.symptom: The hook knife digs in rather than peeling shavings
attrs.cause: Edge is dull, or the blade angle into the wood is too steep
attrs.fix: Strop before resuming. Reduce the blade angle to almost flat on the bowl surface and start with shallower cuts at the bowl rim, working toward the centre.

attrs.symptom: Small checks appear in the bowl after drying
attrs.cause: Uneven wall thickness means thin sections dried faster than thick ones
attrs.fix: Sand lightly and re-oil. In future, check bowl wall evenness by holding the spoon up to a light source: a uniform thickness shows an even translucence.

attrs.symptom: The spoon smells rancid after oiling
attrs.cause: Raw linseed oil took too long to cure, possibly in a damp or cold environment
attrs.fix: Wipe the surface clean with a dry cloth and leave in a warm dry place for one more week. If the smell persists after two weeks, the oil was applied too thickly; sand back and re-oil with a thinner coat.
